advances: This proves the original singleton-row depth estimate on the entire convex moving-box class for the fixed nonzero horizontal-tilt window \(|\beta_i|\le\log(4/3)\), uniformly in every dimension and every coordinate. It extends the zero-horizontal-tilt result by using integer-centered changes of measure in each original weighted row. Arbitrarily larger horizontal tilts and the locked mixed-integer volume conjecture remain unresolved.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The only accepted predecessors used are `57987d5f01c36f91` and `ac9b8b86eb2548d3`, with the parameter and normalization maps given in the proof.
proof:
For each coordinate with \(\beta_i<0\), apply the integer linear reflection \(x_i\mapsto-x_i\). It replaces its lower and upper bounds by \(-u_i\) and \(-l_i\), and replaces \(\beta_i\) by \(-\beta_i\). The new lower bound is convex and the new upper bound is concave. This bijection preserves the original integer lattice, every height, all point weights, and containing closed halfspaces. A center and its halfspace inequalities pull back under the same reflection. It therefore suffices to prove the result assuming
\(0\le\beta_i\le\log(4/3)\). Put \(q_i=e^{-\beta_i}\), so \(3/4\le q_i\le1\).

We first fix all absolute constants. The strict surplus in (8) of accepted `ac9b8b86eb2548d3` is
\(\theta=1/2+e^{-4}/256\). In particular, \(1/2<\theta<3/4\). Define

\[
\alpha=\frac{\log(2\theta)}{2\log12},
\qquad
c_- =\frac56,
\qquad
c_+ =\frac{56}{27},
\qquad
\rho=\frac{(c_+/c_-)^\alpha}{2\theta},
\qquad
C_\alpha=\frac{2}{1-e^{-\alpha}}.
\tag{2}
\]

These quantities are chosen before any dimension or geometric parameter. We have \(0<\alpha<1/4\), because \(1<2\theta<2<\sqrt{12}\). Moreover, \(c_+/c_-=112/45<12\), and hence

\[
\rho<\frac{12^\alpha}{2\theta}
=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\theta}}<1.
\tag{3}
\]

Accepted `ac9b8b86eb2548d3` supplies one absolute positive exponent \(\varepsilon\) for which its estimate (8) holds with this \(\theta\), and one absolute constant \(c_{\mathrm{box}}\in(0,1]\) in its pointwise bound (23). Fix these constants as well. The constant in (1) will be
\(c=c_{\mathrm{box}}(1-\rho)/C_\alpha>0\).

Each coordinate bound is continuous on a compact interval, so \(P\) is bounded and \(D\) is finite. Let \(\mathcal T=[a,b]\cap\mathbb Z\), and let \(E\subseteq\mathcal T\) be the nonempty set of occupied heights. For \(s\in E\), define
\(p_i(s)=\lceil l_i(s)\rceil\) and \(n_i(s)=\lfloor u_i(s)\rfloor-p_i(s)+1\ge1\). The complete original row is exactly

\[
\{I\in D:I_N=s\}
=\prod_{i=1}^n\{p_i(s),p_i(s)+1,\ldots,p_i(s)+n_i(s)-1\}\times\{s\}.
\tag{4}
\]

This is the same meaning of \(\mathcal T,E,p_i,n_i\) as in `57987d5f01c36f91`; its integer dimension is our \(N\), and its number of horizontal coordinates is our \(n\). Formula (4) includes an endpoint when it is an integer. At a zero-width coordinate interval it gives a singleton if the common endpoint is integral and an empty coordinate set otherwise. Empty rows are excluded from \(E\) only for notation, and contribute zero to \(W\).

For every integer \(m\ge0\), write \(Z_m(q)=\sum_{j=0}^m q^j\), agreeing with `ac9b8b86eb2548d3` when \(m\ge1\). Set

\[
\begin{aligned}
w_s&=e^{-(s-h)^2},
&T_i(s)&=q_i^{p_i(s)}Z_{n_i(s)-1}(q_i),
&W_s&=w_s\prod_{i=1}^nT_i(s),\\
Q_i(s)&=
\begin{cases}
q_i^{p_i(s)},&n_i(s)\in\{1,2\},\\
\theta T_i(s),&n_i(s)\ge3,
\end{cases}
&Q_s&=w_s\prod_{i=1}^nQ_i(s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

Thus \(W_s\) is the original row mass, \(W=\sum_{s\in E}W_s\), and all \(Q_s\) are positive. The quantities \(Q_i,Q_s\) are weighted capacities defined here, not the odd-core cardinalities or odd-core masses of `57987d5f01c36f91`.

For every \(s\in E\), there is an original point \(J_s\) in that row whose true same-row containing-closed-halfspace depth satisfies

\[
\inf_{H\ni J_s}
\sum_{\substack{I\in D\cap H\\I_N=s}}w_I
\ge c_{\mathrm{box}}Q_s.
\tag{6}
\]

Here is the exact application of `ac9b8b86eb2548d3`. Translate coordinate \(i\) by the original integer \(p_i(s)\), and put its length parameter in that fact equal to \(m=n_i(s)-1\), with its geometric ratio equal to our \(q_i\). After normalizing by the original row mass \(W_s\), this factor has probability \(p_{m,q_i}(j)=q_i^j/Z_m(q_i)\). A singleton coordinate is deterministic and can be removed when applying the fact. For \(m=1\), choose its endpoint center \(j=0\). The endpoint identity in (2) of that fact is exactly \(\mathcal R_{1,q_i,\varepsilon}(0)=p_{1,q_i}(0)=1/Z_1(q_i)\). Thus its raw factor after multiplying by \(T_i(s)\) is the endpoint weight \(q_i^{p_i(s)}\), exactly as in (5). For \(m\ge2\), (8) of that fact gives
\(\sum_jp_{m,q_i}(j)\mathcal R_{m,q_i,\varepsilon}(j)\ge\theta\), so some original integer center has \(\mathcal R_{m,q_i,\varepsilon}(j)\ge\theta\). Choose such a center separately in every coordinate. The pointwise product estimate (23) of the fact, multiplied by \(W_s\), now gives (6). Singleton factors contribute their whole original mass, and the conclusion also holds if every factor is a singleton because \(c_{\mathrm{box}}\le1\).

The pointwise estimate just used is a bound for every containing closed halfspace in the horizontal coordinate space. Restricting a closed halfspace of \(\mathbb R^N\) through \(J_s\) to the plane of height \(s\) gives either such a closed horizontal halfspace or that entire plane. Thus it gives precisely the infimum in (6), including boundary atoms. At \(n=0\), a row is the single original point of weight \(w_s\), so (6) remains true with empty products.

Put \(L_i(t)=u_i(t)-l_i(t)\), with exactly the width meaning in `57987d5f01c36f91`, and define the positive lower profile \(f_i(t)=e^{-\beta_i(l_i(t)+1)}\). We next establish two coordinate comparisons at occupied heights. At such a height, suppress \(i,s\) and write \(p=\lceil l\rceil\), \(v=n_i(s)\), \(L=u-l\), \(q=e^{-\beta}\), \(T=q^p Z_{v-1}(q)\), and \(Q=Q_i(s)\). The new local symbol \(v\) is just the number of sites \(n_i(s)\); it is not the horizontal dimension. The ceiling relation gives \(0<l+1-p\le1\).

If \(v\le12\), then

\[
f_i(s)\le Q_i(s),
\qquad
T_i(s)\le2Q_i(s)^{1-\alpha}f_i(s)^\alpha.
\tag{7}
\]

For \(v\in\{1,2\}\), one has \(Q/f_i(s)=e^{\beta(l+1-p)}\in[1,e^\beta]\). Consequently

\[
\frac{T}{Q^{1-\alpha}f_i(s)^\alpha}
=Z_{v-1}(q)\left(\frac Q{f_i(s)}\right)^\alpha
\le(1+e^{-\beta})e^{\alpha\beta}\le2.
\tag{8}
\]

For the last inequality, the function on the preceding right-hand side has value two at \(\beta=0\), and the derivative of its logarithm on \([0,\log(4/3)]\) is
\(\alpha-e^{-\beta}/(1+e^{-\beta})\le1/4-3/7<0\). This treats the unbiased two-site interval exactly, without assigning it the surplus \(\theta\).

For \(3\le v\le12\), one has \(Q=\theta T\). Since \(q\ge3/4\),

\[
\frac Q{f_i(s)}
=\theta e^{\beta(l+1-p)}Z_{v-1}(q)
\ge\frac12\left(1+\frac34+\frac9{16}\right)
=\frac{37}{32}>1,
\qquad
\frac Q{f_i(s)}\le\theta\frac43\,12<12.
\tag{9}
\]

It follows that
\(T/(Q^{1-\alpha}f_i(s)^\alpha)\le12^\alpha/\theta=2/\sqrt{2\theta}<2\). Equations (8)--(9) prove both assertions in (7) for every permitted site count.

For \(\beta\ge0\) and \(r\ge0\), define
\(\psi_0(r)=r\) and \(\psi_\beta(r)=(1-e^{-\beta r})/\beta\) when \(\beta>0\). This is a continuous, increasing, concave function of \(r\), vanishes at zero, and is positive when \(r>0\). Whenever \(L_i(s)\ge6\), we claim

\[
c_-\le
\frac{T_i(s)}{f_i(s)\psi_{\beta_i}(L_i(s))}
\le c_+.
\tag{10}
\]

The floor and ceiling bounds give \(L-1\le v\le L+1\). If \(\beta=0\), the ratio in (10) is \(v/L\), which lies between \(5/6\) and \(7/6\). If \(\beta>0\), finite geometric sums give the exact identity

\[
\frac{T}{f_i(s)\psi_\beta(L)}
=e^{\beta(l+1-p)}\frac{\beta}{1-e^{-\beta}}
\frac{\psi_\beta(v)}{\psi_\beta(L)}.
\tag{11}
\]

For any positive \(v,L\), monotonicity and concavity of \(\psi_\beta\), together with \(\psi_\beta(0)=0\), give
\(\min(1,v/L)\le\psi_\beta(v)/\psi_\beta(L)\le\max(1,v/L)\). For example, when \(v\le L\), concavity applied to \(v=(v/L)L+(1-v/L)0\) gives the lower bound and monotonicity gives the upper bound; reversing their roles gives the other case. Also \(1\le\beta/(1-e^{-\beta})\le e^\beta\), using \(1-e^{-\beta}\le\beta\) and \(e^\beta-1\ge\beta\). Thus (11) is at least \(1-1/L\ge5/6\) and at most
\(e^{2\beta}(1+1/L)\le(4/3)^2(7/6)=56/27\). This proves (10), including \(\beta=0\).

At these wide coordinates, \(v\ge L-1\ge5\), so \(Q_i(s)=\theta T_i(s)\). Therefore (10) also gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
T_i(s)
&\le\theta^{\alpha-1}c_+^\alpha
Q_i(s)^{1-\alpha}
\bigl(f_i(s)\psi_{\beta_i}(L_i(s))\bigr)^\alpha,\\
f_i(s)\psi_{\beta_i}(L_i(s))
&\le(\theta c_-)^{-1}Q_i(s).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]

The first inequality follows by writing
\(T_i=\theta^{\alpha-1}Q_i^{1-\alpha}T_i^\alpha\) and applying the upper bound in (10). The second uses its lower bound.

We require the Gaussian profile estimate at the exponent \(\alpha\), on arbitrary occupied subsets. If \(\Phi\) is positive and continuous on a compact interval \([p,q]\), and \(\log\Phi(t)+t^2\) is concave, then every nonempty \(E'\subseteq[p,q]\cap\mathbb Z\) satisfies

\[
\sum_{s\in E'}\Phi(s)^\alpha
\le C_\alpha\max_{s\in E'}\Phi(s)^\alpha.
\tag{13}
\]

Here is a proof that does not replace a sampled maximum by an unsampled value. The case \(p=q\) is immediate. Otherwise set \(g=\log\Phi\) and choose a real maximizer \(\xi\in[p,q]\). Concavity of \(g(t)+t^2\) gives

\[
g((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)
\ge(1-\lambda)g(x)+\lambda g(y)
+\lambda(1-\lambda)(x-y)^2
\quad(0\le\lambda\le1).
\tag{14}
\]

For \(\xi<x<y\), apply (14) to \(\xi,y\) with \(\lambda=(x-\xi)/(y-\xi)\), and use \(g(\xi)\ge g(x)\). Rearrangement gives
\(g(x)-g(y)\ge(y-x)(y-\xi)\ge(y-x)^2\). By continuity the same statement holds for \(x=\xi<y\). Reflection of the interval gives the corresponding inequality on the left of \(\xi\). List the points of \(E'\) at least \(\xi\) in increasing order \(s_0<s_1<\cdots\). Their integer spacing gives \(s_j-s_0\ge j\), so \(\Phi(s_j)^\alpha\le\Phi(s_0)^\alpha e^{-\alpha j^2}\). On the left side, list them in decreasing order and obtain the same bound from the nearest point on that side. Each nonempty side contributes at most its nearest sampled value times
\(\sum_{j\ge0}e^{-\alpha j^2}\le\sum_{j\ge0}e^{-\alpha j}=(1-e^{-\alpha})^{-1}\). Both nearest sampled values are at most the maximum over \(E'\). An empty side contributes zero. This proves (13) with exactly \(C_\alpha\) in (2), allowing gaps and endpoint maxima.

We now use the common-midpoint width pattern construction of accepted `57987d5f01c36f91`, with its \(a,b,l_i,u_i,L_i,\mathcal T\) equal to ours. For completeness, the required properties of that construction are verified here. Put \(\tau=(a+b)/2\), \(M_i=\max_{t\in[a,b]}L_i(t)\), and \(G=\{i:M_i\ge12\}\). Each width is nonnegative and concave. For \(i\in G\), choose a maximizer \(t_i\). If \(t_i\le\tau\), concavity on \([t_i,b]\) gives
\(L_i(\tau)\ge[(b-\tau)/(b-t_i)]M_i\ge M_i/2\). If \(t_i>\tau\), concavity on \([a,t_i]\) gives
\(L_i(\tau)\ge[(\tau-a)/(t_i-a)]M_i\ge M_i/2\). The omitted endpoint contributions are nonnegative. In both cases \(L_i(\tau)\ge6\).

For each \(i\in G\), the superlevel set \(\{t:L_i(t)\ge6\}\) is a closed interval containing \(\tau\). Let \(A_s=\{i\in G:L_i(s)\ge6\}\) for \(s\in\mathcal T\). The sets \(A_s\) are nested increasing through the integer heights \(s\le\tau\), and nested decreasing through the heights \(s>\tau\). Partition each of these two disjoint integer intervals into its maximal nonempty consecutive blocks with fixed \(A_s\), and call the resulting family \(\mathcal B\). For \(B\in\mathcal B\), let \(A_B\) be its fixed set and \(k_B=|A_B|\). Within either nested chain, distinct consecutive sets have strictly different cardinalities. Thus the number of blocks of any given cardinality is at most two:

\[
\bigl|\{B\in\mathcal B:k_B=k\}\bigr|\le2
\quad(0\le k\le n).
\tag{15}
\]

An integer midpoint is assigned only to the left chain. Equal threshold events and all equality rows are included by the definition \(L_i(s)\ge6\).

At an occupied \(s\in B\), every coordinate outside \(A_B\) has at most twelve sites. Indeed, if \(i\notin G\), then \(L_i(s)<12\), so the integer \(n_i(s)\le L_i(s)+1<13\) is at most twelve. If \(i\in G\setminus A_B\), then \(L_i(s)<6\) and the same argument gives at most six sites. Consequently (7) applies outside \(A_B\), and (12) applies inside \(A_B\).

For a block with integer endpoints \(p=\min B\), \(q=\max B\), define the new weighted profile

\[
\Phi_B(t)=e^{-(t-h)^2}
\prod_{i=1}^n f_i(t)
\prod_{i\in A_B}\psi_{\beta_i}(L_i(t))
\qquad(p\le t\le q).
\tag{16}
\]

This \(\Phi_B\) includes the horizontal tilt; it is not the unweighted profile \(F_B\) of `57987d5f01c36f91`. Each wide width is at least six throughout \([p,q]\), because it is at least six at the two endpoints and is concave. Thus \(\Phi_B\) is positive and continuous. Its logarithm plus \(t^2\) equals

\[
2ht-h^2-\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i(l_i(t)+1)
+\sum_{i\in A_B}\log\psi_{\beta_i}(L_i(t)),
\tag{17}
\]

which is concave. The middle terms are concave since \(\beta_i\ge0\) and \(l_i\) is convex. For the last terms, an increasing concave function composed with a concave function is concave: apply monotonicity to the concavity inequality for the inner function, and then concavity to the resulting convex combination. This applies first to \(\psi_{\beta_i}\) and \(L_i\), and then to the increasing concave logarithm and their positive composition. Therefore (13) applies to \(\Phi_B\) on any nonempty occupied subset \(E\cap B\).

Let \(Q_* =\max_{s\in E}Q_s>0\). Fix a block with \(E\cap B\ne\varnothing\), and put \(k=k_B\). Multiplying (7) and (12), keeping the Gaussian factor exactly as \(w_s=w_s^{1-\alpha}w_s^\alpha\), gives for every \(s\in E\cap B\)

\[
\begin{aligned}
W_s
&\le2^{n-k}\theta^{(\alpha-1)k}c_+^{\alpha k}
Q_s^{1-\alpha}\Phi_B(s)^\alpha,\\
\Phi_B(s)&\le(\theta c_-)^{-k}Q_s.
\end{aligned}
\tag{18}
\]

The second inequality uses \(f_i(s)\le Q_i(s)\) outside \(A_B\) and the second inequality in (12) inside it. Since \(0<\alpha<1\), apply (13) and then (18) to obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s\in E\cap B}W_s
&\le2^{n-k}\theta^{(\alpha-1)k}c_+^{\alpha k}
Q_*^{1-\alpha}\sum_{s\in E\cap B}\Phi_B(s)^\alpha\\
&\le C_\alpha2^{n-k}\theta^{(\alpha-1)k}c_+^{\alpha k}
Q_*^{1-\alpha}\bigl((\theta c_-)^{-k}Q_*\bigr)^\alpha\\
&=C_\alpha2^n\rho^k Q_*.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]

An empty occupied subset contributes zero and satisfies the same upper bound. Summing over the exact partition of all original integer heights, using (15) and \(\rho<1\), proves

\[
W\le C_\alpha2^nQ_*\sum_{k=0}^n2\rho^k
\le\frac{2C_\alpha}{1-\rho}\,2^nQ_*.
\tag{20}
\]

Choose \(s^\star\in E\) attaining \(Q_*\) and take its original integer center \(J=J_{s^\star}\) supplied by (6). Every containing closed halfspace then has same-row original mass at least

\[
c_{\mathrm{box}}Q_*
\ge\frac{c_{\mathrm{box}}(1-\rho)}{2C_\alpha}\frac{W}{2^n}
=\frac{c_{\mathrm{box}}(1-\rho)}{C_\alpha}\frac{W}{2^N}
=\frac{cW}{2^N}.
\]

This proves (1). When \(n=0\), every product in the argument is empty, \(E=\mathcal T\), each row is a single original point, and there are at most two blocks of cardinality zero. Equations (6), (13), and (18)--(20) still apply. Zero-width boundary coordinates and arbitrary missing rows were already handled in (4), and every selected center is in the original complete support. Finally, pull back any initial integer coordinate reflections. The conclusion concerns the stated original weights and original closed halfspaces in every case.
statement:
Let \(N\ge1\) be an integer, put \(n=N-1\), and let \(a<b\) be real numbers. For \(1\le i\le n\), let \(l_i,u_i:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) be continuous functions such that \(l_i\) is convex, \(u_i\) is concave, \(l_i(t)\le u_i(t)\) on \([a,b]\), and \(l_i(t)<u_i(t)\) on \((a,b)\). Define

\[
P=\left\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:
a\le t\le b,\quad l_i(t)\le x_i\le u_i(t)\text{ for }1\le i\le n\right\},
\qquad D=P\cap\mathbb Z^N,
\]

and assume \(D\ne\varnothing\). Let \(h\in\mathbb R\), and let the fixed real horizontal coefficients satisfy \(|\beta_i|\le\log(4/3)\). Assign the original weights

\[
w_{(x,s)}=\exp\!\left(-(s-h)^2-\sum_{i=1}^n\beta_i x_i\right),
\qquad
W=\sum_{I\in D}w_I.
\]

There is one absolute constant \(c>0\), independent of all these data, such that some original integer height \(s^\star\) and some original point \(J\in D\) with \(J_N=s^\star\) satisfy

\[
\sum_{\substack{I\in D\cap H\\I_N=s^\star}}w_I
\ge \frac{cW}{2^N}
\quad\text{for every closed halfspace }H\subseteq\mathbb R^N\text{ containing }J.
\tag{1}
\]

The statement includes all boundary points, arbitrary empty integer rows, and \(N=1\), with empty products equal to one. The accepted inputs are `57987d5f01c36f91`, for the common-midpoint width patterns, and `ac9b8b86eb2548d3`, for its pointwise product change-of-measure bound and strict one-dimensional capacity surplus. Their notation and normalizations are identified explicitly below.
